hints: Start by measuring the line X on your printed page in millimetres with a ruler, then think how to change that into micrometres for the calculation.
Recall the magnification triangle linking image size, actual size and magnification, and rearrange it to make actual size the subject.
Divide your image size in micrometres by x4275 and round to one decimal place, checking your units are $\mu m$.
walkthrough:
Measure Image X and Convert Units**
You are sitting with the micrograph, so take a ruler and measure the length of line X in mm. Say you get about 17 to 19 mm. Since the answer must be in micrometres, convert: $1 \text{ mm} = 1000 \text{ } \mu m$, so $18 \text{ mm} = 18 000 \text{ } \mu m$. This is your image size $I$.

Apply Actual = Image Divided by Magnification**
Magnification tells you how many times bigger the image is than real life, so to go backwards you divide. Use $A = I \div M$. With $M = 4275$, that is $A = 18000 \div 4275$.

Calculate and Round Correctly**
Doing the division gives about $4.2 \text{ } \mu m$. Give it to one decimal place with the unit $\mu m$. Different printers give slightly different measurements, so anything from about 3.7 to 4.4 $\mu m$ is fine if your working is shown.

Final answer: actual size = image size $\div$ magnification. e.g. image = 18 mm = 18 000 $\mu m$, $18000 \div 4275 = 4.2$ $\mu m$ to one decimal place (accept 3.7 to 4.4 $\mu m$ depending on print size).

hints: First identify A to E from the picture - A is the large pale nucleus, B is the dark nucleolus inside it, C is a chloroplast with membranes inside, E is the dark line of the wall between cells.
Think where DNA is stored in a plant cell - not just the nucleus, but also in the small circular DNA of photosynthetic organelles.
Think which structure is made almost entirely of cellulose, and which structures must contain membrane phospholipid bilayers.
Recall that histones are the proteins that DNA wraps around to form chromosomes, so they will be where chromosomal DNA is.
walkthrough:
Read the Structures in Fig. 1.1**
A is the nucleus, the large rounded compartment. B is the nucleolus, the dense spot inside the nucleus. C is a chloroplast, recognisable by the internal thylakoid membranes. E is the cell wall forming the boundary between adjacent cells.

Match Each Molecule to Its Home**
DNA is in the nucleus and nucleolus region (A, B) as chromosomes, and also in the chloroplast (C) as small circular chloroplast DNA. Cellulose is the main polysaccharide of the plant cell wall, so E.

Membranes and Chromosome Proteins**
Phospholipids make up all membranes, so the nuclear envelope around A and the chloroplast envelopes and thylakoids in C. Histone proteins package nuclear DNA into chromatin, so they are with nuclear DNA in A and B.
Final answer: DNA - A / B / C; cellulose - E; phospholipid - A / C; histone proteins - A / B.

hints: Look for the two organelles in the picture that make ATP by chemiosmosis - one using light, one using respiration.
walkthrough:
Spot the ATP Makers Visible Here**
ATP is made during photosynthesis in chloroplasts and during aerobic respiration in mitochondria. In Fig. 1.1 you can clearly see many chloroplasts labelled C with internal membranes where the ATP synthase sits. Naming chloroplast (or mitochondrion if visible) earns the mark.

hints: Think where the template for mRNA is kept and where transcription happens before mRNA leaves to the ribosomes.
walkthrough:
Where Transcription Happens**
Messenger RNA is copied from DNA by transcription. In a eukaryotic plant cell that happens in the nucleus where the chromosomal DNA is, then mRNA moves out through nuclear pores to ribosomes. So the answer is nucleus.

hints: Compare what you can see inside the chloroplasts and other organelles here with what a light microscope could show at x400.
Think about the magnification given, the flat 2D look, and the very thin slice needed for electrons to pass through.
walkthrough:
High Resolution Shows Ultrastructure**
A light microscope cannot resolve membranes inside organelles. Here you can see fine detail like the thylakoid membranes and grana inside the chloroplasts labelled C. That level of resolution proves electrons with a very short wavelength were used.

Magnification, Thin Section and 2D Image**
The magnification is x4275, well above the x1500 limit of a light microscope. Also the image is a very thin, flat 2D slice with no 3D surface contours, which is exactly what a transmission beam through a thin section gives.

Final answer: Any two from: high resolution detail visible; internal ultrastructure such as thylakoids / grana in chloroplasts only seen with TEM; high magnification x4275 greater than light microscope; very thin section; flat 2D image with no surface detail.
